catalog_quote: Stress normally falls on the second mora of words with three or more moras, as shown in (3) and (4), which suggests a peninitial pattern. ... a. panóko ‘five’ ... a. simpénoi ‘naked’ ... As can be observed in the data above, there is no evidence to suggest that coda consonants are moraic in the system, because stress does not shift as a function of the presence or absence of codas (e.g., [simpénoi] ‘naked’). ... Observe the bimoraic forms in (5), which have stress on the first vowel: ... a. báɾeŋ ‘bird’ ... This is apparently an avoidance of stress on the final mora in words. ... In terms of stress placement, long vowels are treated as if they were sequences; that is, each vowel portion counts as a stress bearing unit (Hurd & Hurd 1970). Stress therefore falls on the second half of a long vowel in initial position: ... a. taáβi ‘fish’ ... Since the default position for stress is the pen…

SIL International Language and Culture Archives. 24 pp. (fetched sources via Wayback copy of sil.org reapdata URL; direct URL is Cloudflare-challenged)
sources.quote: 'Identical vowels occur in sequences of up to four and are pronounced as varying degrees of length ... there are no individual syllabic peaks unless one of the vowels is stressed, in which case the stressed vowel has a higher pitch. ... Stress is nonphonemic. With words in isolation it occurs on the first syllable of two-syllable words and on the second syllable of words of three or more syllables.' (Their 'syllable' counts each vowel of a VV sequence separately, i.e. = Brown's mora; codas do not add syllables.) Also sec. 11.1: 'anta does not take stress independent of the preceding stem'.
